sections.title: You keep saying the same thing
body: Work with an AI assistant for a while and a pattern shows up. The output is close but not quite right, so you correct it. Next session: the same miss, the same correction.
Use the repository pattern. Don’t comment every line. No raw SQL. Each reminder costs a minute; together they cost hours, and the AI never seems to learn.
sections.caption: The same correction, for the third time.

sections.title: Two causes, two fixes
body: Most misses come down to one of two things.
The AI drifts: it guesses, skips a pattern or makes something up, and you go round in correction loops until it lands.
Or the ask is thin: acceptance criteria, edge cases or scope are missing, so the AI fills the gaps with guesses that look plausible and are not what you meant.
sections.caption: A loop of corrections, or a request full of blanks.

sections.title: Sensei reads your sessions
body: Sensei captures your assistant sessions (Claude Code through its hooks, Zed read-only) and reads them after the fact.

Every follow-up that corrects the AI’s work is a signal: “that’s not what I asked”, “why did you…”, “revert that”. Sensei counts them per session, and only unambiguous ones, so a polite “now also add…” never counts against you. A session with no corrections landed first time, and the share of sessions that do is the number Sensei is judged by.
sections.caption: Corrections picked out of one session.

sections.title: Repeats become rules
body: One correction is noise. The same correction across several sessions is a pattern. Sensei clusters similar corrections and proposes a rule (a memory, in Sensei’s terms) from them.
Once a rule has enough support it goes into use: the AI loads it at the start of each new session for that project, through Sensei’s MCP tools. You stop saying it; the AI starts doing it.
If a later correction contradicts a rule, Sensei records the violation, and a rule that keeps being broken is challenged instead of trusted.
sections.caption: Corrections gather into rules the next session loads.

sections.title: Catch the gaps before work starts
body: Rules fix how the AI works. Thin asks need fixing upstream, before anything is built.

Sensei’s plan depth review holds every piece of work to a bar. Then an adversarial review assumes the plan is wrong and hunts for what was missed: empty states, large inputs, who is allowed to do what.
points: Scope: what is in, and what is out
sections.caption: The depth bar, then reviewers asking what was missed.

sections.title: Every change is measured
body: A rule is a claim: this will help. Sensei checks the claim by comparing how many sessions land first time before and after the change.
A rule that helps is kept and grows stronger. One that makes things worse shows up as a regression, so you can undo it.
sections.caption: Illustrative: first-time sessions before and after a rule.

sections.title: Why I use it
body: I run Sensei on my own work regularly for one reason: I don’t want to spend my time typing the same kind of message again and again.
Start small. Let it capture a week of sessions, look at the corrections it found, and accept the rules that match how you already work.
